_note: THE OBJECT CODEX (D-106 fill-pass). Single source of truth: the dresser places each object where its discovery predicate is true per village; the chronicle reads desc; the Almanac (Fas 5) reads statMeaning. Schema is JsonUtility-friendly (flat fields). requiresTech/requiresCustom empty = no requirement; minPop/minCrafts/minGen = 0 = no threshold. tier = milestone (the discovery-defining object) | dressing (ambient village life) | part (sub-piece). D-107 legibility law: nothing is only decoration. D-112: ruinOnLoss=1 built structures leave a ruin when the tech is lost (stand-in P_PROP_wall_stone_small_02 until the owned Ancient Ruins pack is imported). DESCRIPTION-PRECEDES-OBJECT (spec 1): an entry may carry desc with an EMPTY prefab (told-not-shown) — the chronicle speaks it before the world shows it; add a prefab later and it becomes visible retroactively. Stand-ins flagged: law-stone=rune-rock, temple/manor=City house, anvil=blacksmith-station.

objects.desc: a banner of the sky-faith — a people who learned to read the stars raise their sign over the green
the mill — where the village learned to grind grain, famine receded
a marked post — a people who have learned to write leave words for those who come after
a market stall — where enough hands and crafts gather in one place, goods begin to change hands
a rune-cut standing stone — after too much blood between kin, this people carved their first law into rock: no more killing your own. The Peace of Kin, made to outlast memory.
a temple raised to the sky-faith — the cosmology that began with one soul watching the stars now has a house and a keeper.
a fine great-house set apart — where a family's fortune outgrew its neighbours', the first inequality takes shape in timber and stone.
the forge — where this people learned to work metal, the smith's fire never fully dies
a scholar's scroll — beyond mere writing, this people now reasons about the world and sets its knowledge down to be argued with
a rowboat drawn up at the village edge — a people who learned to build hulls and read the water
a handcart — once the wheel was understood, one back could carry what many had before
a line of drying cloth — a people who learned to spin thread and weave; wool and linen dry in the wind
stores of grain in barrels — the people learned to keep a surplus against the hungry season
fired clay pots — the first craft beyond stone and wood, clay shaped and hardened in the kiln
cut and dressed stone blocks — masonry, the knowledge of shaping stone to build things meant to last
a dug well ringed with stone — the village no longer waits on the river for its water
wooden docks reaching into the water — where the hulls are tied and the day's catch comes in
the iron-worker's anvil and bellows — harder edges than bronze ever gave
a healer's bench of herbs and tinctures — the first medicine, and fewer graves for the fevers
clear glass vessels catching the light — the people learned to melt sand into something you can see through
a board of printed notices — words copied faster than any single hand could write them
a carved statue on the green — a people with hands to spare for beauty, and someone worth remembering in stone
stores and casks stacked by the wall — a settled village keeps more than it can carry
crates stacked beside the path — goods waiting to change hands
a bench by the green — somewhere to sit, and so somewhere to talk
a common fire ring at the heart of the green — where the village gathers when the dark comes
they smelted copper and tin together — bronze, the first metal to hold a working edge (told-not-shown: no model yet; the chronicle speaks it)
they began to weigh coin on the merchant's scales — value made portable, and debt made memory (told-not-shown)
sails turned to the wind on the hill — grinding grain where no river runs (told-not-shown)
